VIDEO.title: The Most Overlooked Miracle in the Bible – and Why You Can’t Miss It!
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: I feel compassion for the crowd.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 15:29-39. Jesus goes along the Sea of Galilee, goes up on the mountain and sits down. Large crowds bring the lame, crippled, blind and mute, and He heals them, so that they glorify the God of Israel. After three days He has compassion on the crowd and feeds four thousand men, besides women and children, with seven loaves and a few small fish; seven large baskets are left over.

Location matters. Mark places this stretch 'within the region of the Decapolis' (Mark 7:31), east of the Jordan and the lake. The video calls the Jordan a kind of boundary between Jews and pagans, so after the Canaanite woman Jesus is again among Gentiles, physically and in what He teaches.
The healings echo Exodus 4:11 and Psalm 146:8: the God of Israel makes the mute and the blind, and He opens the eyes of the blind. The crowd draws the conclusion and glorifies Israel's God.

Jesus Himself asks about the numbers (Mark 8:18-21). The video reads four as the four corners of the earth, so four thousand is the community of the Gentiles; seven loaves and seven baskets speak of completion. It wonders whether the disciples' question assumed Jesus would not show Gentiles the same mercy.
The lesson: because the Lord has compassion on those who don't know Him, He mercifully gives His teaching and Himself to all, not just Jews. The video links this to the Gentile mission in Acts.
QUOTES: And they glorified the God of Israel.
Because the Lord has compassion on those who don't know him, he mercifully gives his teaching and himself to all, not just Jews, to all.
This is a lesson that challenges purity traditions.

method.p: The teacher says location matters. Mark tells us Jesus came 'within the region of the Decapolis' (Mark 7:31); reading Matthew with a map shows who was in the crowd and why the crowd praised 'the God of Israel.'

LSB_QUOTES.text: So the crowd marveled as they saw the mute speaking, the crippled restored, and the lame walking, and the blind seeing; and they glorified the God of Israel.

And Jesus called His disciples to Him, and said, “I feel compassion for the crowd, because they have remained with Me now three days and have nothing to eat; and I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way.”
And they all ate and were satisfied, and they picked up what was left over of the broken pieces, seven large baskets full.

CROWD.title: Within the region of the Decapolis

left.text: And departing from there, Jesus went along by the Sea of Galilee, and having gone up on the mountain, He was sitting there.

right.text: And again He went out from the region of Tyre, and came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, within the region of the Decapolis.

lines.text: Matthew only says 'by the Sea of Galilee'; Mark tells us where: the Decapolis, the ten cities. The video says the Jordan became a kind of boundary between the Jews on the west and the pagans on the east.
Jesus has just withdrawn to Tyre and Sidon (15:21). He keeps moving away from Israel, physically and in what He teaches: after rejecting the Pharisees' purity rules, He goes to Gentiles.

CROWD.title: He went up the mountain and sat

left.text: And departing from there, Jesus went along by the Sea of Galilee, and having gone up on the mountain, He was sitting there.

right.text: Now when Jesus saw the crowds, He went up on the mountain; and after He sat down, His disciples came to Him.

lines.text: Sitting is the posture of a teacher. Jesus has been sitting, which the video says means He was likely teaching the people as well as healing them.
The same words open the Sermon on the Mount (5:1). Large crowds had already come 'from Galilee and the Decapolis' (Matthew 4:25).

CROWD.title: The God who makes the mute and the blind

left.text: And Yahweh said to him, “Who has made man’s mouth? Or who makes him mute or deaf, or seeing or blind? Is it not I, Yahweh?

right.text: Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind; / Yahweh raises up those who are bowed down; / Yahweh loves the righteous;

lines.text: The lame, crippled, blind and mute are healed. The video says the crowd would think of Exodus 4 and Psalm 146 and make the connection: only Yahweh does this.
Isaiah promises the same signs: 'Then the eyes of the blind will be opened' and 'the tongue of the mute will shout for joy' (Isaiah 35:5-6).

CROWD.title: They glorified the God of Israel

src.text: So the crowd marveled as they saw the mute speaking, the crippled restored, and the lame walking, and the blind seeing; and they glorified the God of Israel.

lines.text: 'These are the pagans,' the video says. They don't know Torah, yet they glorify the God of Israel.
Mark's crowd says, 'He has done all things well; He makes even the deaf to hear and the mute to speak' (Mark 7:37).

left.text: And seeing the crowds, He felt compassion for them, because they were distressed and downcast like sheep without a shepherd.

right.text: And Jesus called His disciples to Him, and said, “I feel compassion for the crowd, because they have remained with Me now three days and have nothing to eat; and I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way.”

lines.text: Jesus feeds them with the same meal, loaves and fish. He did it for God's people in chapter 14; now He does it for the Gentiles in chapter 15.

GENTILES.title: Where would we get so many loaves?

src.text: And the disciples *said to Him, “Where would we get so many loaves in this desolate place to satisfy such a large crowd?”

lines.text: They had just seen Him feed five thousand. Could it be, the video asks, that they assumed Jesus would not extend the same mercy to Gentiles as He did to Jews?
It even wonders whether some disciples hesitated to hand bread to pagans, then adds: the text doesn't say it, so I'm not going to make too much of it.

GENTILES.title: Teaching for those who don't know Torah

src.text: and He took the seven loaves and the fish; and giving thanks, He broke them and kept giving them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. And they all ate and were satisfied, and they picked up what was left over of the broken pieces, seven large baskets full.

lines.text: In a Jew's mind, the video says, bread refers to teaching. Jesus gives His perfect teaching to His disciples, and they in turn feed Gentiles with it.
When these Gentiles, who don't know the law of God, eat Jesus' law, there is more than enough left over to keep feeding all the Gentiles.

GENTILES.title: A lesson for the book of Acts

src.text: And opening his mouth, Peter said: “I most truly comprehend now that God is not one to show partiality, but in every nation the one who fears Him and does righteousness is welcome to Him.

lines.text: The video says the disciples have to wrestle with this lesson, especially as it extends into the book of Acts. It challenges purity traditions and preconceived notions of how God operates.
Peter learns it in Cornelius' house (Acts 10). Paul and Barnabas quote Isaiah 49:6: 'I have placed You as a light for the Gentiles' (Acts 13:47).

src.text: when I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces you picked up?” They *said to Him, “Twelve.” “When I broke the seven for the four thousand, how many large baskets full of broken pieces did you pick up?” And they *said to Him, “Seven.” And He was saying to them, “Do you not yet understand?”

lines.text: Jesus calls out the numbers Himself. The two meals are alike, but the number of loaves, people and baskets are different, and that difference is the lesson.
The video repeats its number chart: one for God, two for the tablets, three for the patriarchs or unity, seven for completion, twelve for the tribes, a thousand for a community.
Four is the four corners of the earth, the nations. So four thousand stands for the community of the Gentiles, as five thousand stood for the community of those who follow the books of Moses.
Isaiah speaks of gathering the dispersed 'from the four corners of the earth' (Isaiah 11:12).

left.text: And Jesus *said to them, “How many loaves do you have?” And they said, “Seven, and a few small fish.”

right.text: And they all ate and were satisfied, and they picked up what was left over of the broken pieces, seven large baskets full.

lines.text: Seven stands for completion: Jesus' complete teaching fills the whole Gentile community, with a complete supply left over.
Matthew uses a different word for the baskets here (spyris) than at the five thousand (kophinos); Jesus keeps the two words apart in 16:9-10.
Because the Lord has compassion on those who don't know Him, He mercifully gives His teaching and Himself to all, not just Jews, to all.
The video closes by asking whether we have the mind of Christ on this today, and points again to 15:31: these pagans glorified the God of Israel.

TERMS.def: 'Ten cities': a league of Greek-style cities, mostly east of the Jordan. The captions write 'dicapus' and 'decapus.'
As the video uses it, attaching deeper meaning to numbers. The captions write 'Gamatria.'
A hint back to an Old Testament passage, here Exodus 4:11 and Psalm 146:8.
Rules about clean and unclean; the video says this meal challenges them.
The place Jesus sails to (15:39); Mark has Dalmanutha (Mark 8:10). Both sites are uncertain.

WORDS.gloss: Mute; also deaf. Blunted in speech or hearing.
To feel compassion, to be moved in one's inner parts. Look up: BDAG, σπλαγχνίζομαι.
A large basket or hamper, the kind used to let Paul down a wall (Acts 9:25).
Basket, the word used at the five thousand.
To open (the eyes). Look up: BDB or HALOT, פקח.

BACKGROUND.p: The ten cities, among them Hippos, Gadara, Gerasa and Scythopolis, were Greek in language and culture, with temples to Greek gods. Pliny the Elder lists ten, though ancient lists differ. Pigs were raised there (8:30-32), a sign of a largely Gentile population.

Matthew and Mark record both feedings, and Jesus refers to both (Matthew 16:9-10; Mark 8:19-20). Many readers see the first among Jews and the second among Gentiles, though Matthew does not say so outright.
Matthew's Magadan and Mark's Dalmanutha (Mark 8:10) are otherwise unknown. Some copyists wrote Magdala, the fishing town on the west shore, and many readers place the landing there.

DEBATES.p: Mark's setting in the Decapolis and the phrase 'the God of Israel' lead many to read the crowd as largely Gentile. Others note that Jews also lived in the region and that Matthew does not say so.
Jesus does draw attention to the numbers (16:9-10). Seeing seven as fullness is common; reading four thousand as 'the Gentile community' is the video's own key.
Some critics suggest one event told twice. Matthew and Mark present two, and Jesus speaks of both (Mark 8:19-20).

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video first says 'Exodus 4:1' and then reads verse 11. The verse about the mute and the blind is Exodus 4:11.
'Roman numerals … didn't exist back then' is a slip: Roman numerals did exist. The point is that Arabic numerals (the ones we use today) did not, and Hebrew letters doubled as numbers.
Matthew does not name the Decapolis here; the setting comes from Mark 7:31. The Decapolis also had a city west of the Jordan (Scythopolis).
The chart of number meanings is the video's own; the Bible does not give such a key. What the video calls gematria is broader number symbolism.
The captions write 'Magodan' for Magadan, 'dicapus' and 'decapus' for Decapolis, 'Ty and Sidon' for Tyre and Sidon, and 'Gamatria' for gematria.

QUESTIONS: Why might Matthew place this feeding right after the Canaanite woman?
The crowd glorified 'the God of Israel.' What did they see that led them there?
The video wonders whether the disciples expected less mercy for Gentiles. Whom do you quietly expect God to pass over?
Jesus felt compassion before anyone asked for bread. What does that show about Him?
How far would you take the number symbolism? Where would you be cautious?
Do you have the mind of Christ toward people who don't know Him?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson, stated plainly: because the Lord has compassion on those who don't know Him, He mercifully gives His teaching and Himself to all, not just Jews, to all. This lesson challenges purity traditions and preconceived notions of how God operates. The disciples have to consider not only what God is doing around them but who Jesus is and what He has truly come to this earth to do, a lesson that extends into the book of Acts. These Gentiles did not know Torah, did not know anything, and they glorified the God of Israel. Does this still teach today? Do we have the mind of Christ on this issue today?
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): read Matthew 15:21-39 in one sitting, the Canaanite woman and then the four thousand. Then name one person or group you find hard to imagine at Jesus' table, and pray for them by name this week.

### Ask where you are
The teacher says location matters. Mark tells us Jesus came 'within the region of the Decapolis' (Mark 7:31); reading Matthew with a map shows who was in the crowd and why the crowd praised 'the God of Israel.'

## Four thousand, seven loaves, seven baskets
1. Mark 8:18-21: Do you not remember?
   The key Mark 8:19-21: "when I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets full of broken pieces you picked up?” They *said to Him, “Twelve.” “When I broke the seven for the four thousand, how many large baskets full of broken pieces did you pick up?” And they *said to Him, “Seven.” And He was saying to them, “Do you not yet understand?”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Mark+8:19-21
   (video) Jesus calls out the numbers Himself. The two meals are alike, but the number of loaves, people and baskets are different, and that difference is the lesson.
2. The video's number key: Four corners, four thousand
   (video) The video repeats its number chart: one for God, two for the tablets, three for the patriarchs or unity, seven for completion, twelve for the tribes, a thousand for a community.
   (video) Four is the four corners of the earth, the nations. So four thousand stands for the community of the Gentiles, as five thousand stood for the community of those who follow the books of Moses.
   [Background] Isaiah speaks of gathering the dispersed 'from the four corners of the earth' (Isaiah 11:12). (Isaiah 11:12)
3. Matthew 15:34-37: Seven loaves, seven baskets
   The loaves (Matthew 15:34, LSB): "And Jesus *said to them, “How many loaves do you have?” And they said, “Seven, and a few small fish.”"
   The leftovers (Matthew 15:37, LSB): "And they all ate and were satisfied, and they picked up what was left over of the broken pieces, seven large baskets full."
   (video) Seven stands for completion: Jesus' complete teaching fills the whole Gentile community, with a complete supply left over.
   [Background] Matthew uses a different word for the baskets here (spyris) than at the five thousand (kophinos); Jesus keeps the two words apart in 16:9-10. (Matthew 16:9-10)
4. The lesson: To all, not just Jews
   (video) Because the Lord has compassion on those who don't know Him, He mercifully gives His teaching and Himself to all, not just Jews, to all.
   (video) The video closes by asking whether we have the mind of Christ on this today, and points again to 15:31: these pagans glorified the God of Israel.

## Key people
- The crowds: Gentiles of the Decapolis who bring their sick, stay three days, and glorify the God of Israel. [Background] Mark says some had 'come from a great distance' (Mark 8:3).
- The lame, crippled, blind and mute: Laid at Jesus' feet and healed. [Background] Mark tells of a deaf man with a speech impediment healed with the word 'Ephphatha' (Mark 7:34).
- The disciples: Ask where they could get enough bread; then serve it to Gentiles. [Background] In Mark 8:17 Jesus asks, 'Do you have a hardened heart?'

## Places [Background]
- Magadan (named in the video): Jesus sails to 'the region of Magadan' afterward (15:39); usually linked with Magdala. The captions write 'Magodan.'
- Capernaum: Jesus' base on the north shore.
- Hippos: One of the Decapolis cities, on a ridge above the east shore.
- Gadara: Another Decapolis city, south-east of the lake (8:28).
- Tyre: Where Jesus came from (15:21; Mark 7:31).

## Key terms
- Decapolis: 'Ten cities': a league of Greek-style cities, mostly east of the Jordan. The captions write 'dicapus' and 'decapus.'
- Gentiles: The nations, non-Jews; the video's 'pagans.'
- Gematria: As the video uses it, attaching deeper meaning to numbers. The captions write 'Gamatria.'
- Remez: A hint back to an Old Testament passage, here Exodus 4:11 and Psalm 146:8.
- Purity traditions: Rules about clean and unclean; the video says this meal challenges them.
- Magadan: The place Jesus sails to (15:39); Mark has Dalmanutha (Mark 8:10). Both sites are uncertain. [Background]

## Hebrew and Greek words [Background; Strong's numbers follow the LSB's word tagging]
- κωφός kōphos (G2974, Greek): Mute; also deaf. Blunted in speech or hearing. (Matt 15:30, 31)
- κυλλός kyllos (G2948, Greek): Crippled, maimed (of a limb). (Matt 15:30, 31)
- δοξάζω doxazō (G1392, Greek): To glorify, praise, honor. (Matt 15:31)
- σπλαγχνίζομαι splanchnizomai (G4697, Greek): To feel compassion, to be moved in one's inner parts. Look up: BDAG, σπλαγχνίζομαι. (Matt 15:32; 9:36)
- εὐχαριστέω eucharisteō (G2168, Greek): To give thanks. (Matt 15:36)
- σπυρίς spyris (G4711, Greek): A large basket or hamper, the kind used to let Paul down a wall (Acts 9:25). (Matt 15:37; 16:10)
- κόφινος kophinos (G2894, Greek): Basket, the word used at the five thousand. (Matt 16:9)
- אִלֵּם illem (H483, Hebrew): Mute, unable to speak. (Exod 4:11)
- פָּקַח paqach (H6491, Hebrew): To open (the eyes). Look up: BDB or HALOT, פקח. (Ps 146:8)

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- The Decapolis: The ten cities, among them Hippos, Gadara, Gerasa and Scythopolis, were Greek in language and culture, with temples to Greek gods. Pliny the Elder lists ten, though ancient lists differ. Pigs were raised there (8:30-32), a sign of a largely Gentile population.
- Two feedings: Matthew and Mark record both feedings, and Jesus refers to both (Matthew 16:9-10; Mark 8:19-20). Many readers see the first among Jews and the second among Gentiles, though Matthew does not say so outright.
- Magadan and Dalmanutha: Matthew's Magadan and Mark's Dalmanutha (Mark 8:10) are otherwise unknown. Some copyists wrote Magdala, the fishing town on the west shore, and many readers place the landing there.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "For the multitudes indeed who had come out for healing dared not ask for the loaves; but He, the benevolent and provident one, gives even to them that ask not" Homilies on Matthew 53, on 15:32. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "lest the equality of the miracle should again cast them into forgetfulness, He rouses their recollection by the difference, that by the variation they might be reminded of both one and the other." Homilies on Matthew 53, on 15:37-38. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Was the crowd Gentile? Mark's setting in the Decapolis and the phrase 'the God of Israel' lead many to read the crowd as largely Gentile. Others note that Jews also lived in the region and that Matthew does not say so.
- Do the numbers carry meaning? Jesus does draw attention to the numbers (16:9-10). Seeing seven as fullness is common; reading four thousand as 'the Gentile community' is the video's own key.
- One feeding or two? Some critics suggest one event told twice. Matthew and Mark present two, and Jesus speaks of both (Mark 8:19-20).

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video first says 'Exodus 4:1' and then reads verse 11. The verse about the mute and the blind is Exodus 4:11.
- 'Roman numerals … didn't exist back then' is a slip: Roman numerals did exist. The point is that Arabic numerals (the ones we use today) did not, and Hebrew letters doubled as numbers.
- Matthew does not name the Decapolis here; the setting comes from Mark 7:31. The Decapolis also had a city west of the Jordan (Scythopolis).
- The chart of number meanings is the video's own; the Bible does not give such a key. What the video calls gematria is broader number symbolism.
- The captions write 'Magodan' for Magadan, 'dicapus' and 'decapus' for Decapolis, 'Ty and Sidon' for Tyre and Sidon, and 'Gamatria' for gematria.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why might Matthew place this feeding right after the Canaanite woman?
2. The crowd glorified 'the God of Israel.' What did they see that led them there?
3. The video wonders whether the disciples expected less mercy for Gentiles. Whom do you quietly expect God to pass over?
4. Jesus felt compassion before anyone asked for bread. What does that show about Him?
5. How far would you take the number symbolism? Where would you be cautious?
6. Do you have the mind of Christ toward people who don't know Him?

## Application
- (video) The lesson, stated plainly: because the Lord has compassion on those who don't know Him, He mercifully gives His teaching and Himself to all, not just Jews, to all. This lesson challenges purity traditions and preconceived notions of how God operates. The disciples have to consider not only what God is doing around them but who Jesus is and what He has truly come to this earth to do, a lesson that extends into the book of Acts. These Gentiles did not know Torah, did not know anything, and they glorified the God of Israel. Does this still teach today? Do we have the mind of Christ on this issue today?
- Study note (added): read Matthew 15:21-39 in one sitting, the Canaanite woman and then the four thousand. Then name one person or group you find hard to imagine at Jesus' table, and pray for them by name this week.
